title: Which word is doing the work?

prereqs.why: The four rules about unions and intersections are exactly what is being distinguished here.
Deciding whether the intersection in the counterexample is open means testing one point for an interior ball.

statement:
The rules for combining open and closed sets in a metric space are not
symmetric: one of the four statements below is the one that fails, and the
word **finite** appears in exactly the right places to stop the other three
from failing too.

Exactly one of these is **true**. Which?
hints: Two of the four are rules you can prove in one line from the definition of an open set. Find those first and rule them out.
Try $U_n = \bigl(-\tfrac1n, \tfrac1n\bigr)$ for $n = 1, 2, 3, \dots$. Each one is open. What is their intersection?
Complements turn unions into intersections. If an arbitrary intersection of open sets could fail to be open, what does that say about arbitrary unions of closed sets?

options: An arbitrary intersection of open sets need not be open: $\bigcap_{n\ge1}\bigl(-\tfrac1n,\tfrac1n\bigr) = \{0\}$.
An arbitrary union of open sets need not be open.
An intersection of two open sets need not be open.
An arbitrary intersection of closed sets need not be closed.
